Arizona Trail: Part 4

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2419 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the transition from a double zero back to the trail was especially tough this time around because I was sick.
  • Sources indicate that I stuffed my red bandana, now officially my snot rag, into the water bottle holder on the side of my backpack and set off.
  • With my trusty snot rag in hand, I slowly climbed the mountain, with stunning views gradually revealing themselves along the way.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the transition from a double zero back to the trail was especially tough this time around because I was sick. Seppo and Emma had both come down with colds, and after sleeping next to them in a garage at a trail angel’s house, it seemed the sickness had made its way to me too. It was funny because up until that point, I had been finding the trail relatively easy. The terrain was mostly cruisy, and we weren’t hiking huge miles. I tried to convince myself that getting a cold was just a fun little extra challenge to add to the trail.

Sources indicate that I stuffed my red bandana, now officially my snot rag, into the water bottle holder on the side of my backpack and set off. Everyone had already left camp, but I was moving a little slower given the circumstances. I rapidly caught up to Alex on an uphill, who had somehow remained unaware that we were gaining 5,000 feet that morning. After breaking the news to him, I continued on.

With my trusty snot rag in hand, I slowly climbed the mountain, with stunning views gradually revealing themselves along the way. As I crested the ridgeline, I noticed some concerning dark clouds hovering nearby. Before long, I found myself caught in a mixture of hail and rain. I spotted Seppo and Emma up ahead, who had found a lovely log to sit on. By the time I joined them and started eating lunch, the rain had stopped, giving me a chance to pull out my tent and let it dry.

According to recent reports, alex highlighted up a little while later, and we were both feeling pretty tired and less than thrilled about the morning’s events. After a long lunch break, we continued on, heading back down all the elevation we had just worked so hard to gain. Some people might refer to this as “pointless ups and downs,” or PUDs for short, but I like to think of it as the trail making us work for Mexico.

We moseyed along all afternoon, moving at barely 2 mph despite the fact that it was all downhill. Alex and I chatted about an assortment of topics, ranging from our dream of opening a guiding business to his attempts to teach me about the stock market. As the sun began to set, we decided to aim for the next good campsite. The only problem was that the next good campsite never seemed to come. The terrain was incredibly slanted, and after passing a spot that was barely half the size of our tent and deciding we didn’t want to attempt squeezing into it, we pulled out our headlamps and kept going.

Recent findings suggest that we eventually made it to 21.4 miles before calling it a day at one of the most crowded campsites we’d seen on trail so far. Clearly, we weren’t the only ones struggling to find a decent place to sleep. We squeezed our tent in among eight others, trying to be as quiet as possible since it was already 7 p.m., dark, and everyone else seemed to be fast asleep.

Sources indicate that when I woke up the next morning, I was unsurprisingly still tired and sick. But the sun was shining, and we had 12 downhill miles to cover before lunch. I plugged in my earbuds, put on some Noah Kahan, and started hiking. The halfway mark was calling.

Up ahead, I spotted Kayla, Seppo, and Emma already working on building the 400-mile marker out of rocks. After taking some pictures and celebrating the halfway point, we continued on, the sun warming us with every step.

Industry observers note that the day before, Alex had told me that this was the hardest part of the hike for him. We had just as much trail ahead of us as we had already completed, and that felt daunting. He felt like he was ONLY halfway. I, on the other hand, was feeling sad because we WERE halfway. Having already completed two trails of over 2,000 miles each, this trail was feeling a little too short for my liking. I never wanted it to end.

Sources indicate that later that afternoon, we passed a group of cows that mooed loudly at us before we began another climb. As I gained elevation, the sun started to set, and Emma and I took turns setting the pace up the switchbacks. Seppo and Kayla had booked it up the climb, eager to reach camp before sunset, while we could see Alex far below, just beginning the switchbacks as we approached the ridgeline.

Recent findings suggest that the sunset was gorgeous. With the days getting shorter, we now had the privilege of watching both the sunrise and sunset every single day. This one was especially spectacular. Emma and I kept stopping to take pictures as the sky shifted from orange to pink to purple. With half a mile left to camp, Emma went ahead while I waited for Alex. We finally arrived just as the sun dipped below the horizon.

Recent findings suggest that our campsite was perched on the side of a hill, and the colorful sky soon gave way to a blanket of sparkling stars. We sat in a circle on the ground, eating dinner and enjoying the evening. It was my favorite campsite of the trail so far.

According to recent reports, the next morning, we watched the sunrise over Lake Roosevelt as we made our way down a dirt road. The first 11 miles of the day were spent walking along dirt roads, which are actually some of my favorite miles on trail. I find dirt roads so fun and exciting, which is quite a hot take among thru-hikers. There’s just something about the monotony of a dirt road, kicking up dust with every step and occasionally having an ATV drive by, that makes me feel like a cowboy. Dirt road miles also tend to fly by much quicker than trail miles, and the morning seemed to disappear in no time.

We stopped for a quick lunch at a creek before continuing on. Unfortunately, the afternoon was quite the opposite of the morning and brought some of my least favorite terrain on the trail. It was beautiful, but we spent much of the afternoon walking along washed-out cliffs, with the trail precariously carved into the mountainside. Progress was slow, but I put on some podcasts and tried to zone out rather than overthink just how slowly I was moving.

Recent findings suggest that eventually, I made it to camp and set up our tent on a lovely patch of sandy ground. Once the sun went down, the temperature dropped rapidly, and I was more than grateful to crawl into my sleeping bag for the night.

In the morning, we crossed into the Four Peaks Wilderness and began descending into the low desert. The terrain slowly shifted from high desert shrubs to towering saguaro cacti stretching as far as I could see. Our first saguaros of the trail! This was exactly what I had imagined the entire Arizona Trail would look like. Of course, within the first two days of hiking, I had already realized that wasn’t quite the case. Maybe I should do a little more research before setting off on these trails. Still, I was so stoked to finally be surrounded by some of the oldest cacti in the world.

As we neared the road crossing and our next resupply point, I spotted a black truck with a white camper parked nearby. It looked strangely familiar, and when I reached the road, I realized it was Kayla’s husband doing trail magic! He whipped up smoothies for us, and we happily feasted on fruit and soda. I can confidently say that smoothie was some of the best trail magic I’ve ever had.

Industry observers note that after saying our thanks, we headed over to the Lake Roosevelt Marina for a rather unconventional resupply. The marina was stocked with food geared more toward boaters than thru-hikers, but I managed to make it work. We grabbed a quick burger at the restaurant before heading back out onto the trail. Three miles later, we found a spot to call home for the night.

Recent findings suggest that immediately after leaving camp that morning, we entered a wash and followed it for the first couple miles of the day. The trail through this section was heavily overgrown with spiky bushes, so we decided to follow the more open wash instead. It turned out to be quite fun, weaving our way through the canyon with cacti growing all around us. It felt like a little adventure of its own. The path had been carved out by flowing water over countless years, and we got to walk along the dry remains of that process, making our way over sand and gravel through the canyon.

Recent findings suggest that eventually, the wash narrowed, and we hopped onto a dirt road that led us back to the trail. The road was steep, and we trudged uphill under the exposed sun. After what felt like ages, I finally crested the ridgeline and found myself walking along relatively flat ground, with views stretching out in every direction. It was stunning, but I was having a hard time appreciating the beauty. I was tired and just wasn’t feeling it. I stopped to dump the rocks out of my shoes, and Alex caught up with me. We decided to take a lunch break in the shade. After shoving a tortilla stuffed with pepperoni, cheese, and crushed sour cream and onion chips into my dry mouth, we continued on.

It has been revealed that the afternoon was just as hard as the morning. We continued climbing deeper into the Superstition Mountains, at one point gaining 1,000 feet in just over a mile. It was absolutely brutal, and both Alex and I ran out of water. It was the only time that happened during the entire trail. Eventually, we reached some cruisy downhill, but by then, it was too late. The sun was setting, we’d managed just fifteen miles in nine hours, and I was completely exhausted. We decided to call it an early day and scrolled through the FarOut comments, looking for a flat spot to camp a little farther ahead.

By the time Alex and I arrived at the campsite in the dark, all of our friends and fellow thru-hikers were already set up. It turned out we weren’t the only ones who had struggled that day. Everyone agreed that the 17 miles that day had been the hardest on trail so far.

In a recent development, I woke up grumpy, with the difficulties of the previous day still weighing on my mood. Luckily, the miles came much easier that morning, and I swiftly walked myself out of my funk. There was another storm on the way, the weekly plague of Super El Niño looming over us. Before dropping down into the low desert, I checked the weather report using the lingering one bar of cell service I had. Rain, rain, and more rain. There were over four inches of rain predicted over the following three days. Not exactly ideal hiking weather.

Industry observers note that my brain immediately went into problem-solving mode. What dirt roads could we bail out on? Could we flip south, where the weather might be less severe? Could we road walk along the highway? I didn’t want to take a triple zero, but I also didn’t want to put myself in a dangerous situation by attempting to hike through flash flooding and thunderstorms.

I came up with a initiative and proposed it to Alex, Seppo, and Emma. What if we hiked into town that day, did a super quick resupply and laundry, then hiked out early the following morning? We could crush some miles over the next two days and hopefully reach the next town before the worst of the storm hit. To my surprise, everyone agreed to my slightly crazy plan. I think we were all getting pretty tired of taking zero days just to wait out the storms.

We reached a dirt road crossing, where we met Ace and his dog Charlie. Ace made us pizza and gave us beer before we headed off to walk the last couple of miles into Superior. Little did I know that Ace would become such an vital part of my Arizona Trail experience, but that’s a story for a later blog….

We had the most efficient town stop of my thru-hiking career. It certainly helped that Superior is a tiny town, with pretty much everything a hiker could need within a quarter-mile walk of the motel. We arrived at the motel around 7 p.m. and immediately got to work. We threw our laundry in the washing machine, walked to a Mexican restaurant for dinner, then headed back to the motel to switch everything into the dryer. Next, we walked to Family Dollar to resupply for the next two days. Back at the motel, we collected our clean laundry, showered, and were fast asleep by 10 p.m. Pretty efficient, right?

Recent findings suggest that I fell asleep scrolling through weather reports and studying topo maps of the next section, trying to find potential campsites that weren’t too high and exposed in case of thunderstorms, but also weren’t too low in case of flash flooding. I was nervous, but also excited. Another adventure was just around the corner.

#113831. Adventurer to Climb 100 Peaks on 2,000Km Taiwan Traverse

📅 31 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (654 w)

Adventurer to Climb 100 Peaks on 2,000Km Taiwan Traverse

📅 31 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (654 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that tomorrow, November 1, Japanese adventurer Yoki Tanaka begins a four-month, 2,000km trek north to south down the length of Taiwan.
  • Taiwan has about 268 peaks exceeding 3,000m, but only 100 of them made this special list, which is based not only on height but beauty, difficulty, prominence, and character.
  • Yoki Tanaka arrives in Taiwan earlier this week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that tomorrow, November 1, Japanese adventurer Yoki Tanaka begins a four-month, 2,000km trek north to south down the length of Taiwan. Along the way, he will summit all 100 of Taiwan’s celebrated Baiyue peaks.

Taiwan has about 268 peaks exceeding 3,000m, but only 100 of them made this special list, which is based not only on height but beauty, difficulty, prominence, and character. Prominent Taiwanese mountaineers compiled the list in the early 1970s, partly inspired by Japan’s own list of 100 revered mountains.

Yoki Tanaka arrives in Taiwan earlier this week. Photo: Yoki Tanaka/Instagram.

According to recent reports, the 43-year-old Tanaka has specialized in this unusual combination of long-distance trekking and mountaineering. In 2014, he summited Japan’s 100 famous mountains while walking 7,800km over 208 days. (Japan, though far bigger than Taiwan, has only 23 mountains over 3,000m.) A year later, he extended that by climbing 200 mountains and walking 8,000km in 222 days. Finally, he increased that again to 300 mountains. This time, it took him three years and about 20,000km of walking.

Tanaka’s projected route across Taiwan.

Tanaka will begin on Sunday from the northernmost tip of Taiwan, at the Cape Fugui lighthouse, and finish sometime in March at Eluanbi, the country’s southernmost point. The first 150km will be along roads before he reaches his first trailhead. He’ll spend the next week trekking. His first five peaks will be Xueshan (3,886m), Nanhudashan (3,742m), Hehuanshan (3,417m), Qilaishan (3,560m), and Nenggaoshan 3,262m).

Sources indicate that although he won’t use motorized transport for the entire journey, he will have ample opportunity to resupply along the way. His expedition proposal includes a charmingly precise breakdown of how he looks to spend his evenings: town stays, 48 days; mountain huts, 38 days; tent camping, 39 days. He has also budgeted 16 rest days and 20 contingency days.

According to recent reports, tanaka trains in Taiwan earlier this year. Photo: Yoki Tanaka/Instagram.

In a recent development, his most difficult section, scheduled for early January, will take him through the remote interior of the Central Mountain Range for over two weeks. During this time, he’ll have to carry his own food, search for trails that may no longer exist, and gamble that he will be able to find enough water.

During a December 2025 reconnaissance trip to Xueshan, Taiwan’s second-highest mountain, Tanaka discovered how difficult it can be to obtain water. Two water sources marked on his map were completely dry.

On a previous hike. Photo: Yoki Tanaka/Instagram.

Industry observers note that by late January, the Japanese trekker should reach the historic Batongguan Trail, eventually leading to 3,952m Yushan, Taiwan’s highest mountain. The Batongguan Trail was originally constructed in 1875 under the Qing dynasty to establish a route across the mountainous interior. Decades later, Japanese colonial authorities constructed a separate crossing through the region. Sections of the route survive as remote hiking trails and provide access to some of Taiwan’s highest mountains.

Tanaka first visited Taiwan in the spring of 2025 and has made several reconnaissance visits since, including an east-west crossing of the island earlier this year. He had intended to begin his Taiwan 100 Peaks Traverse project this past spring, but local mountaineers advised him to avoid the rainy season and typhoon risks. Their advice prompted him to shift his starting date to November.

Recent findings suggest that yoki Tanaka on a training hike in Taiwan. Photo: Yoki Tanaka/Instagram.

Interestingly, of Taiwan’s 100 Baiyue peaks, only 99 are now recognized as surpassing 3,000m. The exception is Lushan at 2,981m. It was originally measured at 3,043m but subsequent measurements reduced its elevation. Nevertheless, it remains on the list.

Taiwan’s representative in Japan told Japanese media that the fastest prior completion of the Baiyue by a foreign climber took three years and eight months, spread over multiple trips.

Once Tanaka begins, his expedition website will provide live tracking of his progress across Taiwan.

#113830. Everest 1971: Ambition, Death, and Dispute

📅 31 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1858 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Everest 1971: Ambition, Death, and Dispute

📅 31 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1858 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that in the spring of 1971, only one party attempted to climb Everest.
  • Industry observers note that it was meant to be as much a test of international cooperation as an extraordinary climbing effort.
  • Sources indicate that before the team even arrived in Nepal, the venture was heavily commercialized and advertised to the public.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in the spring of 1971, only one party attempted to climb Everest. Led by Norman Dyhrenfurth and Jimmy Roberts, this ambitious expedition planned to split into two groups. One party would go for the steep Southwest Face, while the other would attempt the West Ridge.

Industry observers note that it was meant to be as much a test of international cooperation as an extraordinary climbing effort. But what happened turned out to be more complicated and controversial than anyone had expected.

Sources indicate that before the team even arrived in Nepal, the venture was heavily commercialized and advertised to the public. The BBC secured exclusive television rights and embedded a nine-person film crew directly into the expedition. At the same time, the British newspaper rights were sold to The Sunday Times, which sent along prominent journalists like Murray Sayle. The media machinery relentlessly hyped the expedition beforehand, boldly framing the climb as a mere formality and setting public expectations for a historic success.

Recent findings suggest that the expedition itself came from a merger of two intends. A British-Norwegian group asked Roberts to lead a Southwest Face attempt. Dyhrenfurth was already organizing the same route, so they joined forces. As the combined team was large, they decided to try two routes at once.

In a recent development, the Southwest Face was the main goal, specifically aiming for a direct, vertical line (a direttissima), while the other group targeted the complete, aesthetic West Ridge route. Both goals were very difficult, and climbers chose their preferred route.

Sources indicate that jimmy Roberts in Nepal. Photo: The Nepal Times.

The Southwest Face team included British climbers Dougal Haston and Don Whillans, Japanese climbers Naomi Uemura and Reizo Ito, and others. The West Ridge team included Austrian Wolfgang Axt, Swiss climbers Michel and Yvette Vaucher, Norwegian climbers Odd Eliassen and Jon Teigland, American David Isles, and Indian Major Harsh Vardhan Bahuguna. Frenchman Pierre Mazeaud and Italian Carlo Mauri later joined the West Ridge side.

In total, the whole expedition had 31 foreign climbers from a dozen countries, as well as several Sherpas, including Ang Phurba and Sonam Girme. According to early planning notes, neither leader had personal summit ambitions. Both described themselves as the older men of the team.

The Southwest Face of Everest. Photo: Wikimedia.

According to recent reports, base Camp was established on March 22, 1971, at 5,425m. Both teams worked through the Khumbu Icefall. Dyhrenfurth later noted it was in the most difficult and dangerous state he had ever seen it. They set up Advance Base Camp on the Western Cwm, then separated.

It has been revealed that the Southwest Face team pushed higher. The West Ridge team, with Axt as coordinator, began setting up their own camps, although supplies arrived slowly. Some of the West Ridge climbers didn’t want to carry heavy loads. A long storm in late April made conditions worse for both teams and delayed everything by two to three weeks. Dyhrenfurth’s own account in the American Alpine Journal confirms the early harmony among the team and the exceptional difficulties of the Icefall that spring.

The 1971 Everest expedition. Photo: ‘Surrender to Everest’/imdb.com.

Industry observers note that on April 18, Bahuguna and Axt of the West Ridge team were descending from a high camp in a storm at about 7,000m. They were not tied to each other. Axt had left his harness and climbing rope higher up to save weight, knowing fixed ropes were already in place. He crossed a long fixed-rope traverse by hand, waited for Bahuguna, saw him wave, then continued down because he was exhausted. He later heard screams and raised the alarm.

A rescue party reached Bahuguna still clipped to the fixed rope, about 25m from easier ground. He had lost a mitten and a crampon, and his face was covered by ice. Attempts to lower him failed in the storm and darkness, and he finally died of cold and exhaustion. Bahuguna’s fingers and face were crusted with ice, his eyes were wide, and he could not recognize Whillans or speak.

Recent findings suggest that major Harsh Vardhan Bahuguna on the West Ridge. Photo: Wolfgang Axt/The Himalayan Journal.

According to Roberts’ report in the Himalayan Database, the rescuers had to leave Bahuguna because it would be completely dark in 10 minutes, and the others would freeze too. Roberts later described the death as the result of a series of mistakes by Bahuguna and Axt themselves, and noted that allowing them to go so high alone had been a factor.

Bahuguna’s body was later recovered and cremated near Base Camp.

Recent findings suggest that dyhrenfurth held an inquiry after the fatal incident. Axt said that the fixed ropes made roping up unnecessary and that he didn’t realize how serious things were until the screams. He later explained that if he had stayed longer, he risked losing his own fingers and toes.

In a recent development, “What should I do? One hour later and I am frozen,” he noted. He added that he couldn’t pull Bahuguna himself and had to go down for fresh men.

Mazeaud called it murder through negligence. Dyhrenfurth agreed that Axt should have gone back to look, but remarked that it was easy to judge after the event. Roberts noted that Bahuguna’s death was very sad but didn’t determine the expedition’s final outcome.

Recent findings suggest that norman Dyhrenfurth, Carlo Mauri, Yvette Vaucher, Reizo Ito, Pierre Mazeaud, and Michale Vaucher in ‘Surrender to Everest’ (1971). Photo: imdb.com.

After the death and the storm, most of the remaining West Ridge climbers (especially Mazeaud, Mauri and the Vauchers) wanted to abandon both hard routes and switch to the normal South Col route. They said that it was more practical and gave a better chance of reaching the summit.

It has been revealed that many others, including most of the Southwest Face group and the leading Sherpas, believed that those climbers mainly wanted personal success: first Frenchman, first Italian, or first woman. A vote that included the Sherpas went strongly in favor of putting all remaining effort into the Southwest Face. The West Ridge group said the decision was a plot to keep them off the summit, so the press would stay focused on the Southwest Face.

Camp 2. Pumori on the left, with snow-and-ice slopes leading to the West Ridge. Photo: Wolfgang Axt/The Himalayan Journal.

Mazeaud’s radio message remarked that they expected him — a French member of parliament — to work like a Sherpa for Anglo-Saxons and Japanese. He said France had been insulted. Yvette Vaucher called the decision monstrous and said she had lost Everest and her friends at the same time.

According to one account, Roberts told Mazeaud to leave during a loud argument. The four went home in early May, ending further work on the West Ridge. Isles and Teigland later stated that the decision to cancel the West Ridge climb, made in a highly emotional moment after Bahuguna’s death, was a great mistake. Teigland said he had dreamed of the West Ridge for two years.

A virus, diagnosed by some as mononucleosis, spread through the camps and forced many climbers down, including Dyhrenfurth. Bad weather continued to block supplies. With the West Ridge group gone and fewer people left, Haston and Whillans kept pushing on the Southwest Face. Japanese climbers and Sherpas carried heavy loads high on the mountain. Camps were placed up to approx. 8,290m.

Haston and Whillans fixed ropes partway into a chimney in the Rock Band but ran out of rope, oxygen, and food. According to Roberts, they placed Camp 6 at 8,290m and were making progress every day. He noted they could have traversed onto the South Buttress and reached the summit that way in one day, but that was not the route they had come to climb. Extreme cold hampered them. They needed another camp higher up. They turned back 450m short of the summit on May 21.

Roberts later remarked weather was the basic cause of failure: Once it goes bad, it affects everything else. He described the expedition as 50 percent successful. They failed to summit, but those who stayed worked well together.

Sources indicate that roberts mentioned that he was bitterly disappointed after three years of work, but apart from Bahuguna’s death, he had nothing to regret. He criticized Schloemmer for contributing almost nothing and said that Axt was asked to come up and help on the Southwest Face but thought it over and went down instead.

According to recent reports, haston called claims that the Austrians were ready to help “complete balls.” He said that when they asked for support at Camp 5, Schloemmer replied that he needed a Sherpa to carry his personal gear. Haston added that he and Whillans were the only ones who could push hard enough to get the route going, and that the Japanese were the only others with real high-Himalayan experience.

In a recent development, uemura remarked that he and Ito helped by carrying loads because that was their obligation, and that if the weather had been good, the expedition could have succeeded. After the 1971 expedition, Uemura decided to always climb solo thereafter.

Axt and Schloemmer complained there was no real authority above Advance Base Camp. Axt stated the two British stayed high for three weeks and monopolized the lead, and that without a coordinator to rotate people, there was no room for others. He said if there had been good organization on the Face, he could have succeeded. Isles and Teigland said the international aspect had nothing to do with the failure.

The problems came from personalities and the emotional decision after the death. Mazeaud and the Vauchers maintained that the leaders had broken the original blueprint of two routes and prevented them from reaching the summit for publicity reasons. Dyhrenfurth said the experiment in international climbing was only partially successful, but cooperation had been good until the argument over the route. He noted that the United Nations had tried international cooperation for a long time and had not done too well, either.

In their interesting and detailed post-climb article titled Post-Mortem of an International Expedition for Mountain magazine (later reprinted by The Himalayan Club), authors Ken Wilson and Mike Pearson traced exactly how the initial merger and massive team size doomed the expedition from the start. They concluded that the 1971 expedition’s collapse was primarily driven by severe natural forces, specifically adverse weather and illness, rather than interpersonal friction. They also attributed systemic blame to organizers for combining distinct climbing factions into an unmanageable, oversized team.

Memorial at Everest in 1971 for Harsh Bahuguna. Photo: Wolfgang Axt/The Himalayan Journal.

Recent findings suggest that the questions remain: Was Bahuguna’s death mainly the result of mistakes by the two men involved, or something the leaders should have prevented? Did the decision to drop the West Ridge and focus on the Southwest Face save the expedition or destroy it? And was the international idea itself the problem, or simply the mix of strong personalities, bad weather, and the pressure of being on Everest?

#113829. Karl Bushby Reaches Mother's House, Ending 28-Year Journey Around the World

Karl Bushby Reaches Mother's House, Ending 28-Year Journey Around the World

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3334 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “This is absolute madness,” said a happy Karl Bushby, as hundreds of people welcomed him home in a civic ceremony in his hometown of Hull, England.
  • The reunion with his mother a couple of hours later was equally public, as the pair were surrounded by TV cameras and hundreds of well-wishers.
  • When Karl Bushby quietly set off from the southern tip of South America on November 1 of that year, it was very different.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“This is absolute madness,” said a happy Karl Bushby, as hundreds of people welcomed him home in a civic ceremony in his hometown of Hull, England. In a scene that couldn’t be more different from the past 28 years that he has spent walking around the world, Bushby stood underneath a giant Welcome Home Karl sign, made an appreciative speech, then begged off to continue walking the final few steps to his mother’s house, which he left back in 1998.

The reunion with his mother a couple of hours later was equally public, as the pair were surrounded by TV cameras and hundreds of well-wishers.

When Karl Bushby quietly set off from the southern tip of South America on November 1 of that year, it was very different. Bushby was 29 years old. He is now 57. When he began, he had around $500 in his pocket, a two-wheeled cart loaded with supplies, and an idea that most people would have dismissed as a fantasy. He was going to walk home to Hull, England, without using any transport. He would not return to the UK until he could do so on foot. He expected the expedition to take about 12 years. Instead, it has taken 28.

Bushby has spent more than 10,000 days and 50,000km pursuing that single objective. The Goliath Expedition has become one of the longest and most unusual human-powered adventures in modern exploration, and he is nervous about it ending. Speaking to The Washington Post as he approached home, he remarked: “My purpose and reason for living is about to end. It’s going to be difficult…trying to blend back into a society that you just don’t know anymore.”.

In a recent development, through Chile’s Atacama Desert. Photo: Karl Bushby.

While serving with the Parachute Regiment, Bushby received a birthday card from his father, Keith, who had served in the British Army. In it was a story about special forces soldiers debating whether it was possible to walk from London to Upcoming York via the Bering Strait. Looking at a world map, Bushby began tracing the route himself.

Sources indicate that but rather than stopping at Upcoming York, he extended the line south through the Americas, all the way to the tip of Chile. The result was an expedition that would take him from the southernmost reaches of South America back to his home in England.

“That was the moment the hairs on the back of your neck stand up,” he told GQ Magazine. “You think, well, that’s it.” He did some calculations, created a timeline on the “back of a beer mat,” and estimated the journey would take him 12 years. From that point, Bushby revealed nothing but determination. At the start, most people doubted it was even possible. That only made him more certain that he wanted to try.

He gave himself two rules. The first was that he could not use any transportation, even self-propelled vehicles like bicycles or kayaks, to advance the expedition. The second was that he could not return to the UK until he had completed the walk. Those rules sound simple. In practice, they created multiple logistical nightmares and affected almost every aspect of his life.

2001, the Darien Gap. Photo: Karl Bushby.

Sources indicate that bushby left Punta Arenas, Chile, with his equipment loaded onto a cart he calls The Beast. He was not an elite endurance athlete embarking on a carefully funded and organized expedition. He was a young former paratrooper with a few hundred dollars, a rough line on a map, and limited resources. He had no supporters or funding, and relied on gas station food or what locals gave him.

“The first years, you’re living the boys’ adventure dream, and it’s great,” he told The Upcoming York Times, “and then it really becomes a grind.”.

The first few years took him north through the Americas, including multiple conflict zones. In Peru, he was attacked by a mob; in Colombia, he floated down the crocodile-laden Atrato River to avoid being spotted by armed men. Then he faced the Darien Gap, that infamously dangerous stretch between Colombia and Panama, ruled by drug and human smugglers, that almost all adventurers skirt around.

Eventually, he reached Panama. But emerging from the jungle did not mean he was free to continue. After crossing a restricted border zone without the necessary visa, he was detained for 18 days.

Industry observers note that after making his way through the Americas, Bushby eventually finished crossing the U.S., where he had picked up a few sponsorships, and reached Alaska. The next major obstacle, and the one that catapulted his journey into world news, was the Bering Strait, the stretch of water separating North America from Russia.

Sources indicate that north America. Photo: Karl Bushby.

Recent findings suggest that the Arctic had already given Bushby a taste of its dangers. During the Alaskan stage of the expedition, he was rescued by helicopter after becoming stranded on an ice floe that broke away from the coast and drifted out to sea, and had a standoff with a polar bear. He knew how risky the Bering Strait crossing would be.

It has been revealed that in March 2006, Bushby and French adventurer Dimitri Kieffer spent 14 days crossing the Bering Strait between Alaska and Russia on foot. With 90kg sleds, they traveled across the shifting ice in temperatures that fell to around -30˚C, against the prevailing winds as the ice moved beneath them.

Wearing dry suits, they had to swim at points through the icy, slushy water. “All night long, you’re just listening to the grinding, and the ice is just like screaming,” he told The Upcoming York Times. “We actually had to evacuate the tent during the night because the thing started to break apart beneath us.”.

In a recent development, they made it across, achieving a rare crossing of one of the world’s most formidable natural barriers. But reaching Russia did not mean the difficulties were over. Russian authorities detained the pair for entering the country without the required permission. They faced the possibility of deportation.

Crossing the Bering Strait. Photo: Karl Bushby.

Russia would consume years of Bushby’s life. He had to leave the country every 90 days because his tourist visa allowed him to stay in Russia for only 90 of every 180 days. Then in 2008, his journey came to a standstill. He lost sponsorship and could not travel to Russia for a few years. In 2011, he resumed his trek, again in 90-day stints. Then in 2012, he was denied a further visa, and in 2013, he received a five-year entry ban from Russia.

Here, Bushby responded with an extraordinary protest. He walked approximately 5,000km from Los Angeles to the Russian Embassy in Washington, D.C., hoping to draw attention to his predicament and secure the paperwork he needed to continue.

Sources indicate that the years of delay exposed another unusual aspect of the expedition. Bushby’s rules did not mean he had to remain indefinitely in the country where he was stuck. Nor did they prevent him from using transport for journeys unrelated to advancing his route home. However, he couldn’t fly back to the UK during these hiatuses.

When visas, funding, or political restrictions prevented him from continuing, he could fly elsewhere, take a break, and wait until circumstances allowed him to resume. But he could not use that flight to skip a section of the route. Whenever he returned, he had to pick up from the exact point where he had stopped. Most of the time, he decamped to Mexico. Its lower cost of living made it a practical place to wait. He also spent time in the United States.

Sources indicate that bushby and Dimitri Kieffer, 2006. Photo: Karl Bushby.

Industry observers note that the distinction mattered enormously to the expedition. Bushby could board a plane to escape a logistical dead end, but when he returned to the route, he had to pick up where he had stopped. He could not simply fly over the awkward section and resume walking on the other side.

Sources indicate that the arrangement might seem to stretch the definition of walking around the world. But for Bushby, it was the only way to maintain his two original rules without spending years of his life waiting at a closed border. Some visa delays took years to resolve. And the longer the journey continued, the harder it became to predict when, or even whether, it would end. Getting across Russia alone took almost 10 years.

He lived cheaply but still needed money to survive on this near-endless journey. Some of it came from the sponsorships he eventually acquired. During what sounded like a particularly low point 15 years ago, on one of his hiatuses in Mexico while trying to overcome another logistical hurdle on his journey, he told Backpacker magazine:.

Industry observers note that I’m 42 years old and I’m broke and I’m homeless. I’m a professional parasite. I’m a professional hobo. I’m sleeping on other people’s couches. I’m 42 years old, and I have to walk other people’s dogs, just so they’ll feed me. My job is picking up dog shit!

The passage of time is one of the most striking aspects of Bushby’s story. His expedition began in an era before smartphones, Instagram, and the expectation of sharing every stage of an adventure online. The young man who left Chile in 1998 could never have imagined that nearly three decades later, people around the world would be following his progress toward his childhood home. The fact that so many people are following it still baffles Bushby.

While Bushby was away, life continued for the people he had left behind. His son, Adam, grew up, and his family had to get on with their lives without him. Adam was eight when he set off. He is now 36, with a family of his own, including a 12-year-old daughter whom Bushby has never met.

Industry observers note that when his dad started the walk, Adam didn’t fully understand what was going on, or know how to explain it to people who asked. Over the years, they have tried to stay in touch and maintain some kind of relationship. At 14, Adam flew to Alaska to see his dad. It was six years after the expedition began and a turning point for him in accepting what Bushby was doing. “I did feel a bit awkward because at that point I didn’t really know my dad,” he told GQ Magazine.

In a recent development, they later spent 10 days walking together as part of a National Geographic documentary project. Adam described the experience as surreal, suddenly stepping into his father’s world. They have spoken regularly since, but as Adam put it: “[His] life went this way, and I went that way, two separate routes.”.

In a recent development, in various interviews, Adam has explained that he had nothing against his father’s ambition, that he respects what he has done and is very proud of him. But also that growing up without him had been difficult.

Sources indicate that karl Bushby has not seen other members of his family for years. He met Adam when he stepped out of the water after crossing the English Channel back to England, but he has not seen his mother in over a decade, even though he will be living with her once he arrives back at his childhood home. He recognizes how difficult the situation will be and that it is due to his choices over the last 30 years.

It has been revealed that “The relationship between me and my son is good, but there’s a lot to resolve there,” he told GQ Magazine. “I’ve got a granddaughter I’ve never seen, and then dear old mother, Lord. I have to live with my mother now. I’m going from a global adventure to living with my mother in a basement at 57. This is going to be a challenge.”.

Life on the road has often been lonely, but Bushby has seen kindness and hospitality in every corner of the globe. “I’ve been welcomed in by the poorest of the poor,” he told The Washington Post. “I’ve met 99.9999% of the very best of humanity. Every culture, every country, has been the same response.”.

Recent findings suggest that he has also had two significant romantic relationships during the expedition. He spent around seven years with a Colombian woman. Later, he had a three-year relationship with a woman from Japan. He met both while on the expedition, and it was also the reason both broke down.

In a recent development, after finally getting across Russia, Bushby continued through Mongolia, where he joined with other adventurers, including Angela Maxwell, to trek across the Gobi Desert with camels. After 1,130km and several disagreements, the group went their separate ways, and Busby continued into China by himself. In 2018, he crossed Kazakhstan and then made his way through Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan. Once again, visa issues ground the journey to a standstill. He could not get into Iran.

At the same time, the world was struck down by the pandemic. More years of waiting in Mexico began, even though Bushby still had a substantial distance to cover. Eventually, in 2022, he was on the move again. Once again joined by Angela Maxwell, he did something he had never intended doing during the expedition — swimming across the Caspian Sea.

Visa issues and geopolitics meant he was unable to cross into Iran. So he came up with a newly introduced proposal. He and Maxwell went back to Uzbekistan and took a different route. They walked across the Kyzylkum Desert until they reached the Caspian Sea. A self-proclaimed terrible swimmer, he was completely outside of his comfort zone. Wearing a wetsuit and flotation equipment, he described his floating-and-swimming hybrid as floatimming. It might not have been the most elegant crossing, but after 32 days at sea, 27 of which he was swimming with Maxwell and two Azerbaijani swimmers in very choppy waters, he completed the 288km swim.

Back on solid ground, his next job was to get across Azerbaijan and into Turkey. Here, he hit a huge milestone. He crossed the Bosphorus Bridge on May 2, 2025. This meant he was back in Europe for the first time since he started walking.

The remaining distance to Britain was comparatively short, but the final stages were not straightforward. Once again, visa restrictions were the thorn in his side. Limited to traveling for 90 days at a time before having to leave Europe, he continued to use Mexico as a base as he waited for his 90 days to reset and tackled the remaining distance in short stretches.

Recent findings suggest that he made it through Turkey, Bulgaria, and Romania before confronting the next concern. Bushby always knew one of the logistical challenges would be getting from France to England. He started trying to pull a plan together. Unsurprisingly, for someone who has walked across the world, his goal was to cross it via the Channel Tunnel. The issue was that this was forbidden. He had hoped to use their service tunnel, but his request was denied.

Industry observers note that karl Bushby speaks at a civic ceremony in Hull, England earlier today. Photo: YouTube.

As he continued walking through Hungary and Austria, he attempted to appeal the decision, reaching out to anyone who might help, to no avail. “We have carefully considered his request and explored a range of possible options. In this instance, regretfully, we are unable to accommodate Mr Bushby’s wishes,” a spokesperson for the Eurotunnel told the BBC. This meant the only alternative was to get back into the water and swim the Channel.

Sources indicate that still walking, he had made it to Germany. Then he picked his way across Belgium and France, all the while decamping to Mexico, Canada, or the U.S. every 90 days, and trying to piece together a plan for swimming the Channel. This proved to be another headache regarding permissions.

French rules stop anyone swimming the Channel from France to Britain. He thought he had been granted an exemption, but in September, he learned that was not the case. After much negotiation, he finally got the go-ahead. On October 5, Bushby finally landed back on British soil at Shakespeare Beach near Dover after swimming the English Channel.

The crossing took three days. He spent around 20 hours in the water, spent the nights on a safety vessel, and dropped back into the water at his last-known position each morning.

Industry observers note that after 28 years abroad, he was finally back in the country he had left in 1998. But rather than feeling joy, he told The New York Times he felt a real sense of loss. After three decades on the road, the prospect of just 400km to go was hugely daunting. “I’m about to lose my purpose for living,” he said. “It’s about to abruptly end.”.

Recent findings suggest that he is nervous about what comes next and reintegrating into a society he no longer knows. He is considering retraining as a teacher, as he loved giving talks in schools as he walked.

One massive question is why Bushby has become so celebrated. He is not the first person to have attempted a long-distance walk around the world. Other adventurers have spent years traveling between countries, crossing continents on foot, or undertaking journeys without motorized transport, but Bushby has singularly captured the world’s attention.

Karl Bushby, back turned, leaves the civic ceremony to walk the last few steps to his mother’s house. Photo: YouTube.

It might be the particular combination of his rules, or the fact that his objective is immediately understandable. He left home, and he is walking back. There is no complicated scientific mission to explain, no specialized equipment that the public needs to understand, and no obscure record category he is aiming for. The simplicity of it gives the story an almost fable-like quality, even though the journey was not simple at all.

According to recent reports, with just two rules, the expedition is relatively easy to follow. Every delay matters because Bushby cannot simply skip ahead. He is forced to wait or find another solution when something blocks his route. The question becomes how he will get around it without abandoning his principles.

Then there is the sheer amount of time it has taken. People who first encountered Bushby’s expedition in their twenties are now well into middle age themselves. Initially, there were no updates on social media. Instead, there was the odd news article that cropped up every few years about the same man, still walking across the world. A story that seemed like an ambitious adventure morphed into an entire adult life on the road.

Bushby has not necessarily made the journey look enjoyable. His progress has depended as much, if not more, on navigating bureaucracy and finding support as on putting one foot in front of the other. Despite it all, he continued.

As the journey has hit an era where we can follow an adventurer’s progress in real time, every obstacle and milestone has renewed interest in the question that has followed Bushby for 28 years: Will he actually make it home?

In a recent development, now that he has to confront a new question: How do you cope with coming home after three decades? “I will have to figure out who I am again. What is the meaning to it all? How do I find that meaning and purpose? How do I fill that hole I’m suddenly going to find myself in?” he told the BBC in the days before the expected end of the expedition. “I think the old adage goes…the only thing worse than a man who can’t fulfill his dreams is a man who’s fulfilled his dreams…because then what?”.

Everest and Ama Dablam Climbs Resume Despite Cyclone

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (593 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the second cyclone to hit Nepal’s mountains this season caused heavy snowfall last weekend, but its briefer stay has affected climbers and trekkers less.
  • In a recent development, no cyclone seems enough to deter the Russian team on Everest for very long.
  • In a recent development, the climbers’ latest foray up Everest’s West Ridge route.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the second cyclone to hit Nepal’s mountains this season caused heavy snowfall last weekend, but its briefer stay has affected climbers and trekkers less. As the sun returned this afternoon, fresh snow hampered smaller teams on 6,000m and 7,000m peaks, but the highly supported expeditions on Ama Dablam are proceeding with barely a hitch.

In a recent development, no cyclone seems enough to deter the Russian team on Everest for very long. Leader Andrei Vasiliev told us yesterday from Kathmandu that he, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov will return to the mountain in one or two days. The trio is well aware of the challenge they face on Everest’s West Ridge, completely alone and without oxygen.

In a recent development, the climbers’ latest foray up Everest’s West Ridge route. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

Vasiliev mentioned he is under some pressure due to unidentified “unsolved matters” but still determined to tackle the climb. In his own words:.

According to recent reports, we know what needs to be done; the path is clear, and we must attempt to follow it. We’ve fallen ill. A massive amount of snow has fallen. You adapt quickly to new conditions. Once we’re back in the snow, the cold, and the cramped tent, it will feel as though things were never any other way.

According to recent reports, the fresh snow dump has thwarted some teams attempting Baruntse (7,129m) in the Khumbu. Jan McManus of Ireland was among them, and he has called off his expedition after failing to reach Camp 1 due to deep snow:.

It is unclear whether other climbers on the peak may still be trying. There were six large teams totaling 65 foreign climbers with permits for Baruntse.

On Himlung (7,126m), teams hurried to summit and get down and safely away before the cyclone hit. During the previous snowstorm at the end of September, a massive avalanche buried Base Camp, killing 16 staff members. Despite the tragedy, one of the deadliest in Nepal’s mountaineering history, the peak remained open, and guided teams came in large numbers to the mountain a couple of weeks after the accident. A total of 130 foreigners had permits. Teams summited on October 25 and 26, and then left the area.

Ama Dablam Base Camp is also covered in snow, but the commercial teams will nevertheless resume climbing soon. According to Jana Schneider of Germany, climbing with 14 Peaks Expeditions, a Sherpa team is on its way to reopen those sections where fresh snow has buried the ropes. “If all goes well, my summit push begins Nov 4 until Nov 6,” she wrote.

In a recent development, so far, 410 foreigners have applied for a permit to climb Ama Dablam. A Sherpa team first fixed the route on October 17, and dozens have summited since then. Despite the break forced by bad weather over the weekend, summits should continue throughout November.

Industry observers note that one climber has perished on the mountain so far, and there have been some close calls. Paul Clarke of Australia and Xenia Santha of Hungary climbed Ama Dablam after attempting Dhaulagiri earlier this season. Their summit push was delayed as they found a 25-year-old climber in a serious situation at Camp 2. Santha and Clarke, who climbed without Sherpa support, gave the climber dexamethasone, spent the night with him, and helped organize an emergency airlift for the following morning. They continued to the summit one day later.

Sources indicate that A high camp on Ama Dablam. Photo: Xenia Shanta.

#113827. Bear Tracks All Over the Arizona Trail

Bear Tracks All Over the Arizona Trail

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2871 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that this morning we woke up bright and early at our tent site right beside the trail.
  • By the time the sun came up this morning we had already been walking for a while.
  • In a recent development, the views this morning were unbelievable.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that this morning we woke up bright and early at our tent site right beside the trail. I was really hoping that we were going to get surprised last night by Leaf at some point, but she never did wind up catching up to us. At least today she’ll be heading into town from a trailhead less than 20 miles from where we were camped. So, she isn’t too far from a road, a town, and some hiking friends. I made coffee this morning pretty early and then laid in my tent for a while. Then the two of us got packed up and were walking on the trail before the sun was up. There isn’t too much awaiting us along the trail up ahead. Today we will be going past that major trailhead and highway crossing about 19 miles into the day. But other than that, it is just going to be us and the trail for the next few days. Depending on how far we go today and tomorrow, we’ll hopefully be able to head into town the following evening to resupply and recharge.

A small bear track in the muddy red clay.

By the time the sun came up this morning we had already been walking for a while. And the trail actually had some fun surprises for us. Thanks to all of the rain, the trail had been covered in mud for the last couple of days. Which meant that any animal that hiked through the area would leave deep footprints in the trail. We got to follow the path of a bear which had been walking through this area in the last couple of days. It left behind such clear footprints in the red clay mud. It was cool to see the larger prints left behind by its back feet. This section of the trail was beautiful all on its own, but the prints in the mud added something special to it all.

In a recent development, the views this morning were unbelievable. After all of the rain the red clay has the most incredible, deep color to it. And all of the trees and plants are vibrant and lush.

Sources indicate that for the first hour or two of the day the trail was a dark red clay, complimented quite well by the lush pine trees and other shrubs surrounding the trail. The rising sun lit up the rocky mountainside off in the distance and made the red clay glow. That was a stunning way to start off the morning. We had some gradual climbing to do and continued to see bear prints along the trail on and off. If I was a bear, I would also love to follow the trail. It is a perfect path through the wilderness! It’s also one reason why some hikers prefer to set up their camp a little way off the trail at night. In the night, the trail is an animal highway through the woods. You never know what you’ll see if you follow a trail through the dark.

I liked the way that the layer of clouds off in the distance was resting right above the mountain range. The Arizona Trail sure had a lot of trees today!

In a recent development, lucky for us, the mud wasn’t too bad this morning. Most of the moisture had been sucked in to the earth already. Leaving behind only the deep, saturated color that the water left behind. These sections of red clay are some of my favorites here in Arizona. The color looks incredible right beside the deep greens that we are able to enjoy thanks to all of the rain. I’ve had a lot of people reach out to say that the red clay typically doesn’t look nearly as vibrant as it does right now. All of the rain makes the color all the deeper, which I’m quite thankful for.

One particular stretch of trail that walked along a large red rock hillside.

Over the course of the morning the trail was following along a large cluster of rocks off in the distance. Some of them were shaped like tall, jagged chimneys. I really enjoyed the view as we got even closer to the rocks, before eventually the trail veered off. We actually ran into some people on the trail today as well. There are a ton of road crossings and trailhead throughout this area. One guy was out doing some trail maintenance scouting. I’m sure that the individuals doing trail maintenance through this area have their work cut out for them with all of the rain and flash flooding. An entire section of trail can so easily get washed away if enough water pours through an area. We’ve been lucky so far with the state of the trail. But there have definitely been a lot of sections and areas with fresh rock fall.

Clouds starting to roll in off in the distance. I thought we were going to get poured on! But as we stood on top of a ridge, we could see the storm blowing off and away from us.

By the late morning the temperature dropped a bit, and some dark clouds began to roll in. I hadn’t seen any rain in the forecast, but it certainly seemed like we had some coming for us. We stopped on top of a hill for a quick break, and each put our rain gear on while we watched it pour down off in the distance. It made me think about Leaf behind us, and all of our friends up ahead of us. The storm managed to skirt right on by us, and it hardly rained more than a sprinkle. But we could tell that someone somewhere was getting rained on. It felt nice to keep the rain gear on as we continued along, at least for a little while. We watched as the bulk of the storm blew by us and the skies got bright and blue off in the distance up ahead.

For a mile or two the trail slowly approached this cluster of unique rocks. A couple of them look like stone pillars.

Sources indicate that as we got closer to the trailhead and highway crossing, we did wind up getting rained on a bit. Which was surprising because the rain started just as the skies turned blue! It was only a sprinkle though. I used my sun umbrella to stay dry and the rain passed quickly. Though, even just a light rain caused the mud on the trail to build back up again. I’m just hoping that the mud won’t be too bad for the rest of the day. Prior to reaching the trailhead, we ran into a couple more day hikers and one person on horseback with another horse being pulled behind them. The second horse had the cutest little pink saddle on. Then it wasn’t long until we reached the trailhead as well.

These bright yellow wildflowers have been growing all along the trail.

Arizona Trail signs near the trailhead about 20 miles into our day.

For some reason it always feels exciting to pass by a trailhead, even if you aren’t heading into town. Perhaps it’s the possibility of receiving some trail magic there or having something else eventful occur. When we actually passed by the trailhead though there was hardly anyone around and we just continued along. And we only made it another mile or two before we encountered the next obstacle ahead of us. There was another deep river crossing for us to ford! This one was quite easy in comparison to our river crossing yesterday. We walked around to see if there was any way that we could avoid getting our feet wet, but there was not. So, we both plunged in and got our shoes and socks soaked. Then sat on the other side of the river to enjoy a lunch break.

After Slide and I crossed the river, we sat here in the grass to eat lunch.

According to recent reports, the sky was still dark off in the distance and it certainly felt like it was going to rain at some point. Both of us figured this would be a good time to stop and eat, just in case the rain did start up. I had packed out one of those tasty bite tikka masala meals which I enjoyed there. Those always do a great job of filling me up. Then I cleaned out my socks and shoes and debated on whether or not I should put my rain gear back on. We were going to begin going uphill, so I knew I was going to get super-hot in rain gear. But if it’s windy at all then I still get wet when I’m using just my umbrella. I decided to opt against it and just figured that if the rain did start and was heavy, I could just stop and put my rain jacket on later.

In the early evening the trail briefly followed along this massive slab of rock. It reminded me of sections of the Appalachian Trail in Upcoming York.

The rain wound up holding off as we continued along. It sprinkled on us briefly but didn’t persist. Once we left the river, we did have a bit of climbing to do. Then we were up on top of the nearby hill and just continued along up there. In some places the trail itself was just a massive boulder beneath the ground. We had some open and exposed views, and the weather was nice and cool. It felt like we had gotten pretty lucky already for the day. It wouldn’t be long before I had to get my feet wet again in yet another small stream crossing. I probably could have tried harder and kept my feet dry, but it felt like a lot of work. I also always have the strong memory in my mind of slipping on a rock in a river crossing in Northern California on the PCT and breaking 2 of my fingers last year. All to avoid getting my feet wet! I actually wound up getting more wet than I would have if I just crossed through the river normally, because I slipped and fell. Of course, at the time I didn’t realize that I’d broken 2 of my fingers. But 4 months later I still couldn’t apply any pressure to the two fingers on my right hand, so it feels like a safe assumption now.

In a recent development, A photo that Slide took of me when we were on top of this ridge. The trail stayed up there for the rest of the evening and the views just got better and better.

Sources indicate that as we continued along the trail was pretty rocky, but in exchange we were graced with some great views. The trail went through some areas with vibrant foliage as well. The leaves were a perfect spectrum of light greens, yellows, oranges, and deep reds. It reminds me so much of hiking in Colorado this time of year. We even saw a bunch more bear prints along the trail over the course of the evening. And some prints that appeared to be a large dog. They definitely didn’t look like mountain lion prints, in my opinion. I’m not sure what else they could be besides a dog!

I figured these were just substantial dog prints, but I still like the way that they looked in the mud.

Industry observers note that by the time that the sun began to set we were up top of a ridge and would be continuing along it for the rest of the evening. The sun cast an incredible glow across the wheat grass and other plants surrounding the trail. There were loads of bright yellow wildflowers and prickly pear cacti throughout the area as well. It was a really beautiful way to end off the day. Sometime after 5PM we passed my favorite bear prints of the entire day. There were some prints which were incredibly deep and had standing water inside of them. It just really highlighted how massive the prints were. I wonder where this bear was going, and if it was the same bear whose prints we saw earlier on in the day. I’m sure it’s not, but bears can travel very far in a day if they want to.

Perfectly defined bear prints right on the trail.

In the early evening, we entered into the Mazatzal Wilderness in the Tonto National Forest. At this point the sun was just starting to go down, and the sky was putting on quite the show for us. The trail got much rockier in this section and there were way more cacti lining the trail as well. The timing wasn’t great, because we would be looking for camping sometime soon. When the trail is lined in rocks and cacti it can be hard to find a place to set up your tent. As we walked, I snacked on some pistachios and enjoyed the views. We were in the perfect place to be able to enjoy the sunset this evening.

The sun was beginning to set, and we were in the perfect place to enjoy it.

The trail stayed pretty much the same for the rest of the night. There were rocks all over the place and a ton of cacti. Camping options seemed limited at best, if not nonexistent. But we just kept our eyes peeled for any area with less rocks and some flat ground. Just after it got dark, we did wind up finding an area just off the trail which didn’t seem too bad. It was a little rocky and lumpy but was definitely much better than what we had been seeing. It was hard to imagine that we would find anything much better than this anytime soon. So, we decided to just call it a day then and there. We both got our tents set up, and it was a great feeling to take off my shoes and socks. They weren’t soaked, but they definitely weren’t dry. The worst part about wet shoes and socks, in opinion, is putting them back on the next morning. Especially when it is cold out! It could take my breath away.

Enjoying that last bit of light before the sun completely dipped behind the mountains off in the distance.

In a recent development, once my tent was up, I got comfortable inside and ate something. Then did my stretching routine before calling it a night. We made it 31 miles today which was pretty good. Sure, we could have gone a bit further to make our life easier tomorrow and the next day. But we certainly didn’t need to. I think we’ll wind up having another early start tomorrow morning which will make up for it. There is a ton of elevation gain tomorrow, so I’m curious to see how that goes.

Industry observers note that if you enjoyed this blog and would like to support my hike by buying me a soda or a snack along the way, there is a “Tip the Author” button below! It links directly to my Venmo. Any and all support is incredibly appreciated!

The tall wheatgrass looked almost pink under the glow of those cotton candy clouds.

This was easily one of the best views that I’ve had the pleasure of enjoying thus far on the Arizona Trail. The sunsets and sunrises out here have been fantastic.

I’m a thru hiker who has hiked 23,000+ miles in the last few years. In 2025 I became the 1st known woman to hike the “Border to Border” Calendar Year Triple Crown & complete over 10,000 miles of hiking in 1 year. In 2023 I became the 2nd known woman to hike the Eastern Continental Trail from Key West, Florida to Newfoundland Canada. I completed my Double Triple Crown between 2022-2025.

Sources indicate that thanks for all the posts so we could catch up with you on your hike. I was good of you to be concerned about Leaf, but it seems that she chose to lag behind and to hike by herself, like you like to do at times.

How does a person really get in to thru hiking ? My question isn’t so much about physical prep or gear prep but more in regards to the actual timeline and logistics of planning the adventure? I live in southern Oregon and have always wanted to do the PCT. However life and career and family have always taken priority.

An Indian passenger died and two more were injured when two helicopters crashed while landing near Everest Base Camp this morning.

The helicopters were operated by Fishtail Air and Air Dynasty, two of Nepal’s largest companies. The crash occurred at the helipad on the outskirts of the village of Pheriche (4,371m). It’s a typical spot for helicopters to stop and refuel when on their way to and from Everest Base Camp.

According to recent reports, as shown in the horrific video below, the two helicopters came from different directions, and both tried to land at the same time. Somehow their rotor blades collided. The inexplicable crash occurred in a wide, flat area with good visibility.

Vasanth Kumar, an Indian trekker, died on the spot, The Tourism Times reported. Shailesh Kishan from Latest Zealand and Rabindra Prajapati, a senior captain, were seriously injured. Both have been airlifted to hospitals in Kathmandu. They were all on board the Fishtail Air helicopter. The Air Dynasty chopper was carrying cargo.

#113825. Tech Report: Newly introduced Route Attempt on Lunag Ri Falls Just Short of Summit

📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (625 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Newly introduced Route Attempt on Lunag Ri Falls Just Short of Summit

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (625 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, between October 23 and 27, Alexander Parfenov and Alexander Semenov of Russia opened a demanding fresh route on 6,895m Lunag Ri in the Rolwaling Himal on the Nepal-Tibet border.
  • The pair climbed a previously unexplored southeast-facing buttress of the Lunag Ri massif.
  • They placed a piton on the final part of the pillar and began rappelling from there, reaching the base of the wall on October 28, according to gore-ljudje.net.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, between October 23 and 27, Alexander Parfenov and Alexander Semenov of Russia opened a demanding fresh route on 6,895m Lunag Ri in the Rolwaling Himal on the Nepal-Tibet border. They turned back short of the summit, which some sources list as 6,907m.

The pair climbed a previously unexplored southeast-facing buttress of the Lunag Ri massif. The line would have ended on the southeast summit. It involved mixed and rock climbing to M6, aid sections of A2–A3, ice up to WI5–WI6 in places, and long stretches of steep snow with limited protection.

They placed a piton on the final part of the pillar and began rappelling from there, reaching the base of the wall on October 28, according to gore-ljudje.net. The duo turned back short of the summit due to a coming storm and health problems. The complex summit area — multiple closely linked peaks and ridge features — also left some uncertainty about how close they came to the main summit.

Even without summiting, this was a significant exploration of a major, unclimbed feature on a remote peak.

The newly introduced line opened by the Parfenov and Semenov. Photo: Alexander Parfenov.

In a recent development, lunag Ri, the highest peak in the Lunag massif, has long stood as one of Nepal’s highest unclimbed summits. Early attention focused on the broader massif after Joe Puryear and David Gottlieb made the first ascent of the neighboring 6,778m Jobo Rinjang via its South Face in 2009.

In the same year, a Swiss-led team under Stephane Schaffter attempted lines in the area, including approaches to Lunag I, though their claims about summits on the massif were later met with skepticism in the American Alpine Journal.

According to recent reports, in the autumn of 2010, a French team that included Max Belleville, Mathieu Detrie, Mathieu Maynadier, and Sebastien Ratel climbed the southeast face of Lunag Ri. Their route, Close the Door (1,200 m, IV/5 F5), was completed in a three-day alpine-style push with two bivouacs. They reached a distinct southeast top (6,812m to 6,830m) on the long ridge connecting Lunag I to Jobo Rinjang. By this time, they were exhausted and did not continue the short remaining traverse to the higher main summit. This remains the only major completed route on the Lunag I massif before the first ascent of the true summit.

Recent findings suggest that from the recent climb on Lunag Ri. Photo: Alexander Parfenov.

Sources indicate that attention then shifted to the west ridge and southwest face of the main peak. In November 2015, Conrad Anker and David Lama’s alpine-style attempt reached a high point roughly 300m below the summit before retreating due to the unexpected complexity of the ridge.

They returned in 2016 to try a similar line. On the first day, at about 5,800m, Anker suffered a heart attack and was evacuated by helicopter. Lama subsequently continued alone on a variation that moved farther right onto an icefield. He established two bivouacs and pushed 50m higher than the previous year’s high point before turning around 250m shy of the summit.

In late October 2018, Lama returned solo. Over three days (October 23-25), with two bivouacs, he climbed the southwest face and northwest/west ridge (1,500m of vertical gain, terrain to 90°). He moved mostly ropeless, with limited self-belaying on the harder mixed sections. Lama negotiated the previously unclimbed headwall and made the final exposed traverse onto the main summit.

It has been revealed that this was the first ascent of Lunag Ri’s highest point. He descended largely by rappelling down the line of ascent. Lama was awarded a Piolet d’Or for this solo first ascent of Lunag Ri.

From the recent climb on Lunag Ri. Photo: Alexander Parfenov.

Breaking: Floating Alone Down the Brahmaputra on a Bamboo Raft

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (428 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Indian mountaineer and adventurer Shekhar Bordoloi has just started a solo expedition down the Brahmaputra River.
  • According to recent reports, this won’t be Bordoloi’s first time down the river.
  • It has been revealed that bordoloi on a previous raft expedition on the Brahmaputra.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Indian mountaineer and adventurer Shekhar Bordoloi has just started a solo expedition down the Brahmaputra River. He set off on a homemade on a bamboo raft from the Dhola–Sadiya Bridge on November 1 and aims to finish at Dhubri, 891km later. The route covers the entire Brahmaputra within India and should take 22 to 25 days in all. The river begins in Tibet and continues beyond India into Bangladesh, covering 2,900km in all.

According to recent reports, this won’t be Bordoloi’s first time down the river. In 2020, he and two friends took a similar bamboo raft down a 400km section of the Brahmaputra. Earlier, in 2015, Bordoloi was one of 11 who tackled another part of the river over 11 days under the auspices of the Assam Mountaineering Association. This expedition, however, will test his endurance, pitting him against river conditions for longer, and with less support, than ever before.

It has been revealed that bordoloi on a previous raft expedition on the Brahmaputra. This raft took Bordoloi and friends from the world’s largest river island, Umananda, to its smallest, Majuli. Photo: Shekhar Bordoloi/Instagram.

Bordoloi’s raft was hand-built from bamboo poles carefully lashed together over several days. Such craft are a traditional way of navigating rivers across the region, and are still used by local communities for fishing and transportation.

Though the river can be temperamental, Bordoloi’s first two days have been relatively calm, taking him down the Lohit, one of the Brahmaputra’s many tributaries and channels. Navigating the complex river system alone will be a challenge. The Brahmaputra is one of the largest river systems in India, the ninth-largest in the world by discharge, and is prone to flooding and powerful currents.

But according to Bordoloi, those obscure, winding corridors are at the heart of this project. Many sections of the river remain underexplored, and he believes there is hidden potential for the people in his home region of Assam. If he can map routes for river tourism and model environmentally responsible river navigation through those routes, he hopes to draw attention to this important riverine ecosystem and the economic opportunities for the people living along it.

Industry observers note that the logistical challenges of a long expedition will further complicate progress. On previous expeditions, Bordoloi traveled with minimal supplies or no food at all, relying entirely on foraging and knowledge of the natural landscape. But this adventure will take over twice as long and may put those skills to their limits.

Bordoloi is documenting his daily progress on Facebook and Instagram.

#113823. Details, Video of Jugal II First Ascent
